data.text:
All 13 scenarios hold, so I wrote `{"findings": []}` to `findings.json`.

- **Where the mapping lives:** this change edits specs only, and the patch has no code in it. Each new delta spec (rust-agents, rust-approve and the other ten) has a `<!-- source: crates/{kernel,features}/<name>/** -->` glob under `Code ownership`. The modified rust-workspace delta now owns only `crates/apps/cli/**`. Every directory these globs name exists under `crates/`.
- **What resolves it:** the linter's existing `owned-once` rule (`crates/kernel/linter/src/gates/owned_once.rs`) flags any file with zero owners or more than one.
- **What tests it:** `repository_passes_the_link_gates` in `crates/kernel/linter/tests/link_gates_corpus.rs` runs that rule with the change's deltas applied when `OSQ_CHANGE` is set. Since rust-workspace no longer claims these crates, each one's only owner is the capability named after it. A missing glob would leave files with no owner, and a leftover rust-workspace glob would give them two, so either mistake fails the test.

**Caveat:** that test never names the owning capability; it only requires exactly one owner. The mapping is right only because the globs make the per-crate capability the only possible owner. I also didn't count `passes_without_change`, because the change adds the spec files that declare the mapping, not new behavior in base code. On base, the test passes because rust-workspace owned everything.

I relied on the executor's claim that the corpus test passed and didn't re-run it; the rules forbid running tests.
